prerequisites: Complete courses 1.1 and 1.2: both domain controllers healthy and replicating, and DNS verified on both, so every member can find a domain controller by name.

Work at each domain controller's VM console with an authorized Domain Admin account — until course 1.8 builds AdminJumpBox01, that is where administration happens — and have access to the hypervisor settings for both controller VMs.
Continue the sbd.test example: SBD-DC01 (10.0.10.10) holds the PDC emulator role and SBD-DC02 is 10.0.10.11, both on VLAN 10.
Have an approved time reference that never connects to this network, such as a GPS receiver's display, and a log to record each check.
The network's routing and VLAN segmentation are already in place, with a documented service-path register.
labNote: This network has no internet time. SBD-DC01, the PDC emulator, serves time from its own clock, an administrator checks that clock against an approved reference, and everything else follows the domain hierarchy. For the member checks, use a domain-joined Windows test client or member server if you have one (SBD-DC02 shows the same chain if not); the Linux settings in lesson 3 are filed now and applied by the courses that build each Linux server. Thresholds and intervals below are sample decisions — record your own.

lessons.title: Plan the domain's time
lessons.summary: Every sign-in, log entry and certificate in this network depends on clocks that agree, and an air-gapped network has no internet time to lean on. Learn why time matters here and how the Windows Time hierarchy carries one clock from SBD-DC01 to every system, then write down the reference, the thresholds and the service path you will hold the domain to.
steps: Start with why the clocks must agree. Kerberos refuses a request whose timestamp differs from the domain controller's clock by more than the domain's tolerance — five minutes by default — so drift turns into failed sign-ins and failed replication. The logging courses (1.10–1.12) line events up across systems by their timestamps, certificates from the course 1.6 PKI are valid only between two fixed times, and domain controllers need agreeing clocks to replicate accurately.

Learn the hierarchy that carries one clock everywhere. The PDC emulator of the forest root domain is at the top; every other domain controller takes its time from the PDC emulator, and every member server and workstation from the domain controller that authenticated it — the NT5DS client type every domain member uses by default. sbd.test is the forest's only domain, so SBD-DC01 is the top and SBD-DC02 follows it, and each Windows member's time arrives signed with its computer's Net Logon session key.

Face the air gap. With no internet or outside NTP server, SBD-DC01 serves time from its own clock and is the reference by declaration, so name an approved reference that never connects to this network, such as a GPS receiver's display, and write down who compares SBD-DC01 with it, how often, and how a correction is made and recorded. Record the fallback too: if SBD-DC01 is lost for long, SBD-DC02 eventually stops advertising as a time source, so the PDC emulator role moves to it and it becomes the source (lesson 5).

Set the thresholds you will hold. Keep every system within one second of SBD-DC01 — the one-second difference DISA's operating-system requirements use for synchronizing with an authoritative source — and SBD-DC01 within two seconds of the reference, checked daily and after every restart, restore or revert, or at an interval its measured drift has shown it stays inside. Five minutes is where Kerberos fails; these thresholds exist to catch drift long before that.

Confirm the service path. Rule F09 in Inside the Network permits every domain member to both controllers on UDP 123, and each controller's inbound firewall rule for the Windows Time service accepts it; SBD-DC02's own requests to SBD-DC01 stay inside VLAN 10, where only the host firewalls see them. SBD-REPO01 (course 1.9) is not a domain member, so F09 does not list it yet; course 1.9 adds it.
lessons.command:
Get-ADForest | Select-Object RootDomain, Domains       # sbd.test: the forest root and its only domain
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object PDCEmulator               # expected: SBD-DC01.sbd.test
# The domain's Kerberos tolerance, from the Default Domain Policy (expected: MaxClockSkew = 5, in minutes)
Select-String -Pattern MaxClockSkew -Path "\\sbd.test\SYSVOL\sbd.test\Policies\{31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9}\MACHINE\Microsoft\Windows NT\SecEdit\GptTmpl.inf"
# Each controller's inbound UDP 123 rule, and where each takes its time today
Invoke-Command SBD-DC01,SBD-DC02 {
  Get-NetFirewallPortFilter -PolicyStore ActiveStore | Where-Object { $_.Protocol -eq 'UDP' -and $_.LocalPort -contains '123' } |
    Get-NetFirewallRule | Select-Object DisplayName, Direction, Enabled, Action
  w32tm /query /source }
lessons.check: The plan names the forest root and its PDC emulator, the hierarchy each system follows, the approved reference with who checks it and how often, both thresholds, the fallback, the Kerberos tolerance read from the Default Domain Policy, and rule F09 with each controller's inbound UDP 123 rule.
lessons.evidence: Keep the time plan with the output behind it: the forest root and PDC emulator, the reference and checking procedure, both thresholds and the check interval, the fallback, MaxClockSkew, rule F09, both controllers' UDP 123 firewall rules, and each controller's time source before you change anything.
objectives: Explain why Kerberos, log correlation, certificates and replication need clocks that agree.
Trace the Windows Time hierarchy from the forest root's PDC emulator to every member.
Record the reference, the thresholds, the fallback and the service path the domain's time is held to.

quizzes.question: The domain tolerates five minutes of clock difference. Why hold every system to one second?
answers: Kerberos fails at one second
Five minutes is where sign-ins fail; a tight threshold catches drift long before that and keeps events from different systems in order
w32tm can't measure a larger offset
quizzes.explanation: Kerberos's tolerance is the failure point, not a target. A one-second threshold gives warning while there is time to act, and timelines you can trust in the logging courses.

quizzes.question: In the default hierarchy, where does SBD-DC02 get its time?
answers: From the PDC emulator, SBD-DC01
From its hypervisor host
From whichever member authenticated last
quizzes.explanation: Domain controllers take time from the PDC emulator and members from a domain controller. The forest root's PDC emulator takes it from its own source — here, its own clock.

quizzes.question: Why can't a Linux server get the signed time that Windows members get?
answers: The controllers refuse Linux clients
Linux can't use UDP 123
Windows signs domain time with each computer's Net Logon session key, a Microsoft extension chrony doesn't use as a client
quizzes.explanation: Linux servers take unsigned NTP from the same controllers. That is one reason the time path stays narrow: two controllers, one rule, UDP 123.

recap: Kerberos fails past five minutes; the one- and two-second thresholds catch drift long before that.
One hierarchy: SBD-DC01, then SBD-DC02, then every member, with Linux servers pointed at both controllers.
The reference, its checks, the fallback and rule F09 are written down before anything changes.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 makes SBD-DC01 the reliable source and takes the hypervisor out of both controllers' time.

model.label: Sign in, step 3
model.text: The workstation's Kerberos request carries a timestamp, and the domain controller refuses it if the two clocks are too far apart.

lessons.title: Make SBD-DC01 the domain's time source
lessons.summary: With no outside time to lean on, the domain's clock is whatever SBD-DC01 says, so make that a deliberate, checked configuration. Take the hypervisor out of both controllers' time, mark SBD-DC01 — the PDC emulator — as the reliable source serving its own clock with no external peer, and run the first check against the approved reference.
steps: Confirm which domain controller holds the PDC emulator role — SBD-DC01 in this sample. The PDC emulator of the forest root domain sits at the top of the Windows Time hierarchy, so it is the one system you configure; everything else follows it.

Turn off the hypervisor's time synchronization for both controller VMs — SBD-DC01 on SBD-HV01 and SBD-DC02 on SBD-HV02 — so no host clock can silently override the PDC emulator. On Hyper-V that is the Time synchronization integration service; other hypervisors have an equivalent guest-tools setting, and some also set the guest clock after a resume or restore, so check those settings too. Inside each guest, w32tm /query /source must no longer name a hypervisor provider such as VM IC Time Synchronization Provider.

On SBD-DC01, mark Windows Time as a reliable time source and restart the service. w32tm /config /reliable:yes writes AnnounceFlags 5 — always a time server (0x1) and always a reliable one (0x4) — in place of the automatic default, 10 (0x2 and 0x8). Leave the client type at NT5DS and add no manual peer: the forest root's PDC emulator has nothing above it, so it serves its own clock, and clients accept time from a server that synchronizes with nothing only because it is marked reliable.

Read what SBD-DC01 now advertises: source Local CMOS Clock, stratum 1, reference ID LOCL, and a root dispersion of 10 seconds — the default LocalClockDispersion for a local clock, which you leave alone (lesson 3 sets the Linux servers to accept it). Expect Time-Service warning 12, which says the forest root's PDC emulator has nothing above it and will act as the authoritative source: that is the designed state, so record it rather than fix it. nltest /dsgetdc:sbd.test /gtimeserv should return SBD-DC01 with the GTIMESERV flag, the reliable time server Net Logon now advertises.

Run the first reference check with lesson 1's procedure: read the approved reference and SBD-DC01's clock at the same moment and record both. Correct only past the threshold, by the measured difference (Set-Date -Adjust), never by typing a time from memory; Security event 4616 records the change, and your log records who made it and why.
lessons.command:
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object PDCEmulator   # expected: SBD-DC01.sbd.test
# Hyper-V example (other hypervisors have an equivalent setting). On SBD-HV01, and the same for SBD-DC02 on SBD-HV02:
Disable-VMIntegrationService -VMName SBD-DC01 -Name 'Time Synchronization'
Get-VMIntegrationService -VMName SBD-DC01 -Name 'Time Synchronization'   # Enabled: False
# On SBD-DC01 (the PDC emulator): the reliable source, serving its own clock
w32tm /config /reliable:yes /update
Restart-Service w32time
w32tm /query /configuration   # AnnounceFlags: 5 (Local); NtpClient Type: NT5DS (Local)
w32tm /query /source          # Local CMOS Clock
w32tm /query /status          # Stratum: 1, ReferenceId: LOCL, Root Dispersion: 10s
nltest /dsgetdc:sbd.test /gtimeserv   # DC: \\SBD-DC01.sbd.test; Flags include GTIMESERV
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; ProviderName='Microsoft-Windows-Time-Service'; Id=12} -MaxEvents 1 |
  Format-List TimeCreated, Message
# Reference check: run this as you read the approved reference, and log both readings
Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.fff K'
# Only past the threshold, by the measured difference (example: SBD-DC01 two seconds slow):
# Set-Date -Adjust ([TimeSpan]::FromSeconds(2))
lessons.check: Hypervisor time synchronization is off for both controller VMs; SBD-DC01 reports AnnounceFlags 5 and NT5DS, source Local CMOS Clock, stratum 1 and reference LOCL; nltest returns it with the GTIMESERV flag; event 12 is recorded as expected; and the first reference check is logged inside the threshold, or with its correction.
lessons.evidence: Record the hypervisor setting for both controller VMs; SBD-DC01's configuration, source and status output; the nltest result; the event 12 text; and the first reference check — both readings, the difference, any correction with its 4616 event, who and when.
objectives: Configure SBD-DC01, the PDC emulator, as the domain's reliable time source.
Turn off hypervisor time synchronization for both domain controller VMs.
Run and record the first check of SBD-DC01's clock against the approved reference.

quizzes.question: Which system is the domain's authoritative time source in this design?
answers: Every domain member individually
SBD-DC01, the domain controller holding the PDC emulator role
The offline root CA
quizzes.explanation: The PDC emulator of the forest root domain is the top of the Windows Time hierarchy. Marking it reliable makes it the source everything else follows.

quizzes.question: What does the air gap change about time design?
answers: Nothing — pool.ntp.org still works
Kerberos stops needing accurate time
There is no internet source, so DC01's clock is the reference by declaration and how it is checked is a documented decision
quizzes.explanation: With no external source, accuracy is whatever the lab declares and monitors — which is why the time-stamp controls (AU-8, SC-45) land on the PDC emulator.

quizzes.question: Why does time matter to authentication at all?
answers: Kerberos rejects tickets outside its allowed clock skew, so drifting clocks become sign-in failures
DNS records expire hourly
Passwords change with the clock
quizzes.explanation: Kerberos builds replay protection on timestamps. Skew beyond the tolerance breaks authentication before anything looks wrong.

quizzes.question: Why turn off the hypervisor's time synchronization for the domain controller virtual machines?
answers: It saves processor time
Windows Time will not start otherwise
The host clock would silently override the PDC emulator and fight the domain hierarchy
quizzes.explanation: A virtual machine that takes time from its host has two masters. Turning host sync off leaves the domain hierarchy, rooted at the PDC emulator, as the only authority.

quizzes.question: Where does a domain workstation get its time in this design?
answers: From SBD-DC01 only, set by hand on each machine
From a domain controller over UDP 123, following the domain hierarchy
From the core router
quizzes.explanation: Windows Time follows the domain hierarchy: members sync from a domain controller, the other domain controller from the PDC emulator, and the PDC emulator from its own clock. That is why rule F09 permits UDP 123 from every domain member to both domain controllers.

recap: SBD-DC01, the PDC emulator, is the declared source: AnnounceFlags 5, its own clock, no external peer.
No hypervisor sets either controller's clock.
The first reference check is logged, and any correction was made by the measured difference.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 brings SBD-DC02, the Windows members and the Linux servers onto this source, and keeps Group Policy out of the way.

model.label: SBD-DC01
model.text: The PDC emulator, its address, and the time rule every domain member follows.

lessons.title: Bring every system onto the hierarchy
lessons.summary: One source is only useful if every other clock follows it and nothing quietly overrides that. Leave SBD-DC02 and the Windows members on the domain hierarchy's defaults, keep Group Policy and hypervisors out of their time, and write the chrony configuration every Linux server in later courses uses to follow both controllers.
steps: Leave SBD-DC02 and every Windows member on the defaults: client type NT5DS, no manual peer list, and on SBD-DC02 the automatic AnnounceFlags 10, so it serves time without claiming to be the reliable source. w32tm /query /configuration shows each value with where it came from, (Local) or (Policy), and a system someone once set by hand returns with w32tm /config /syncfromflags:domhier /update and a restart of the service.

Keep time out of Group Policy. The Windows Time Service policies (Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Windows Time Service) overwrite the local W32Time settings, so one that names an NTP server or sets the type to NTP pulls its targets off the hierarchy, and one that reaches SBD-DC01 overrides what makes it the source. Leave them Not Configured in every GPO, the STIG GPOs of courses 1.4–1.5 included: the STIGs expect members on the domain hierarchy, and their rule that the PDC emulator take time from an authorized external source becomes a recorded deviation in course 1.5's exception record.

Keep hypervisors out of every virtual machine's time, as you did for the controllers. When a later course builds a virtual machine, server or client — SBD-ADMIN-PC01, the Tier 2 seat on SBD-ADMIN-SRV01, included — turn off its hypervisor time synchronization, so the domain stays the only time authority: a Windows guest whose source reads VM IC Time Synchronization Provider, or any other hypervisor provider, is not following the domain.

Write the chrony configuration every Linux server uses. In /etc/chrony.conf (RHEL family) or /etc/chrony/chrony.conf (Ubuntu), remove every pool, server and sourcedir line, add server SBD-DC01.sbd.test iburst, server SBD-DC02.sbd.test iburst and maxdistance 16, and add no allow line, because these servers serve time to no one. Domain-joined Linux servers authenticate with Kerberos through SSSD, so the same five-minute limit applies to them; ntpd, where a distribution still uses it, takes the same two server lines and tos maxdist 16.

Record why maxdistance 16 is this path's choice. Serving its own clock, SBD-DC01 advertises 10 seconds of root dispersion and SBD-DC02 a little more, while chrony refuses any source whose root distance is above 3 seconds by default, so without the line chronyc sources marks both controllers ^? (unusable). Sixteen seconds is the largest dispersion NTP defines, so the setting admits both controllers without admitting an unsynchronized source; the time itself is unsigned, which is why F09 limits it to the two controllers.

Apply the same file to every Linux server before its first domain join or package update: SBD-REPO01 (course 1.9), which is not domain-joined, so F09's member list leaves it out until course 1.9 adds it; SBD-SPLUNK01 (course 1.12) and SBD-WEB01 (course 1.18) when they are built; and SBD-NESSUS01 when course 1.17, coming soon, arrives. The offline root CA (course 1.6) is the one clock no network reaches: set it against the approved reference before each signing ceremony.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-DC02, and on a Windows test client or member server if you have one:
w32tm /query /configuration | Select-String 'AnnounceFlags|Type:'   # SBD-DC02: AnnounceFlags: 10 (Local); Type: NT5DS (Local)
w32tm /query /configuration | Select-String '\(Policy\)'           # expected: no output
w32tm /query /source                                                # a controller, never a hypervisor provider
# A system once set by hand returns to the hierarchy:
#   w32tm /config /syncfromflags:domhier /update; Restart-Service w32time; w32tm /resync /rediscover
# The Linux chrony file, filed now (/etc/chrony.conf, or /etc/chrony/chrony.conf on Ubuntu):
#   server SBD-DC01.sbd.test iburst
#   server SBD-DC02.sbd.test iburst
#   maxdistance 16
# ...with no pool, other server, sourcedir or allow lines. Each Linux build later checks:
#   chronyc sources -v     # ^* one controller, ^+ or ^- the other (^? = unusable)
#   chronyc ntpdata | grep -E '^(Remote address|Stratum|Root dispersion|Authenticated)'
#   chronyc tracking       # Reference ID: a controller; System time well inside one second
lessons.check: SBD-DC02 shows AnnounceFlags 10 and NT5DS and takes its time from SBD-DC01, a Windows member names a controller, no W32Time value shows (Policy), and the chrony file — both controllers, maxdistance 16 and the reason for it — is filed for courses 1.9, 1.12 and 1.18 to apply.
lessons.evidence: Keep SBD-DC02's and the member's configuration and source output, the empty (Policy) search, the rule that no VM takes its time from its host, and the filed chrony configuration with the reason for maxdistance 16 and the systems that will use it.
objectives: Keep SBD-DC02 and every Windows member on the domain hierarchy, with nothing from Group Policy or a hypervisor overriding it.
Write the chrony configuration every Linux server uses to follow both controllers, and explain maxdistance 16.
Account for the systems outside the domain hierarchy: SBD-REPO01 and the offline root CA.

quizzes.question: A member's w32tm /query /configuration shows Type: NTP (Policy). What does that tell you?
answers: The member follows the domain hierarchy normally
Its hypervisor set the value
A Group Policy object has moved the member off the domain hierarchy, and a local change won't override it
quizzes.explanation: (Policy) means the value comes from Group Policy, which overwrites the local W32Time settings. Find the GPO and set its Windows Time policies back to Not Configured.

quizzes.question: Without maxdistance 16, chronyc sources marks both controllers ^?. Why?
answers: Serving SBD-DC01's own clock, the controllers advertise about 10 seconds of root dispersion, above chrony's 3-second default limit
The core blocks UDP 123 from Linux servers
chrony can't talk to a Windows time server
quizzes.explanation: The packets arrive; chrony rejects the sources for the error they advertise. Raising the limit to 16 seconds, the largest dispersion NTP defines, admits both controllers and nothing unsynchronized.

quizzes.question: Why must course 1.9 add SBD-REPO01 to rule F09?
answers: It uses a different time protocol
Rule F09 covers domain members, and SBD-REPO01 is not joined to the domain
It takes its time from SBD-MGMT01
quizzes.explanation: F09 was written for domain members. Course 1.9 adds SBD-REPO01 to it with an owner and a reason, and gives it the same chrony file as every other Linux server.

recap: SBD-DC02 and the Windows members run on defaults, and nothing shows (Policy).
Every VM takes its time from the domain, never from its host.
One chrony file — both controllers, maxdistance 16 — serves every Linux server, SBD-REPO01 included.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 proves the chain: each link's source, offsets against the thresholds, and the events worth keeping.

model.label: SBD-SPLUNK01
model.text: A domain-joined Linux server: its permitted connections include F09, the time row the chrony file in this lesson will use.

lessons.title: Prove the time chain
lessons.summary: A source you configured is a claim until every link answers to it. Read each system's source and status, measure offsets against the thresholds from lesson 1, and keep the events and readings that let an assessor see the time chain for themselves.
steps: Read each link's source and status, from the top down. SBD-DC01 reports Local CMOS Clock at stratum 1, SBD-DC02 reports SBD-DC01.sbd.test at stratum 2, and a member reports a controller at stratum 2 or 3; a member showing Local CMOS Clock, Free-running System Clock or a hypervisor provider is not following the domain (lesson 5).

Measure the controllers against each other: w32tm /monitor queries each controller in the domain, marks the PDC emulator, and reports every other controller's NTP offset from it. SBD-DC02 should sit well inside one second; the ICMP line is only a ping, and the NTP offset is the measurement.

Measure a member from the member itself: w32tm /stripchart against SBD-DC01 takes timed samples of its offset, and five of them inside one second meet the threshold. On a Linux server later, chronyc tracking reports the same measure as System time, beside a root dispersion of about 10 seconds that is the controllers' advertised error, not an offset.

Keep the Time-Service events that tell the chain's story, from the System log: 12 on SBD-DC01 (it serves as the authoritative source), 35 and 37 on the followers (a source chosen, valid time arriving), and 36, 129 and 142 as warnings worth an alert (no synchronization for a long period, no domain source found, a controller no longer advertising as a time source). Security event 4616 records every change to a clock, your reference corrections included; list these for the event set course 1.10 collects.

Write the dated evidence record: for each system, its source, stratum and measured offset against its threshold, plus its time zone, since audit time stamps must be in UTC or carry their offset; then the event extracts, the reference check log, and who ran each check. Repeat the offset checks after any change to a controller.
lessons.command:
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\time -Force | Out-Null
$f = "C:\Evidence\time\$env:COMPUTERNAME-$(Get-Date -Format yyyyMMdd)"
# On SBD-DC01, SBD-DC02 and a member:
w32tm /query /source | Out-File "$f-source.txt"
w32tm /query /status | Out-File "$f-status.txt"
w32tm /tz | Out-File "$f-tz.txt"
# On a controller: each controller's NTP offset from the PDC emulator
w32tm /monitor /domain:sbd.test | Out-File "$f-monitor.txt"
# On the member: five timed samples against SBD-DC01
w32tm /stripchart /computer:SBD-DC01.sbd.test /samples:5 /dataonly | Out-File "$f-stripchart.txt"
# The Time-Service events to keep, and every clock change (4616)
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; ProviderName='Microsoft-Windows-Time-Service'; Id=12,35,36,37,129,142} -MaxEvents 50 |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, Message | Export-Csv "$f-time-events.csv" -NoTypeInformation
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4616} -MaxEvents 20 |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Message | Export-Csv "$f-4616.csv" -NoTypeInformation
lessons.check: Every link reports the expected source and stratum, w32tm /monitor shows SBD-DC02 well inside one second of the PDC emulator, the member's five samples sit inside one second of SBD-DC01, the event extract holds the designed events with every warning explained, and the reference check log is current.
lessons.evidence: Keep the dated source, status, time zone, monitor and stripchart files from C:\Evidence\time, the Time-Service and 4616 extracts, the reference check log, and a one-page statement of each threshold beside the result measured against it.
objectives: Confirm each link's source and stratum, from SBD-DC01 down to a member.
Measure controller and member offsets against the thresholds from lesson 1.
Keep the Time-Service events and readings that make up the time evidence record.

quizzes.question: w32tm /query /source on a member returns Free-running System Clock. What does that mean?
answers: The member has become a reliable source
The member isn't synchronizing from the domain; it is running on its own clock
The member is synchronized with SBD-DC01
quizzes.explanation: A member should name a domain controller. Its own clock as the source means the hierarchy failed for this system, and lesson 5 finds out why.

quizzes.question: w32tm /monitor shows SBD-DC02 at +0.0021s. What has that proved?
answers: That every member is inside the threshold
That SBD-DC01 agrees with the approved reference
That SBD-DC02 agreed with the PDC emulator to about two milliseconds at that moment
quizzes.explanation: Each measurement proves one link at one time. Members need their own samples, and SBD-DC01's accuracy comes only from the reference check.

quizzes.question: Which record shows that someone changed SBD-DC01's clock by hand?
answers: Security event 4616, alongside the reference check log
Time-Service event 37
The w32tm /monitor output
quizzes.explanation: Event 4616 records each change to the system time and the account that made it. The log adds why: the readings, the difference and the threshold.

recap: Each link names the right source: Local CMOS Clock at the top, a controller everywhere else.
Offsets are measured against one second, not assumed.
Sources, offsets, events and the reference log form one dated record.
lessons.next: Lesson 5 finds and fixes time faults — skew, a member off its source, a moved role, a restored VM — and records the fix.

model.label: Turn an event into evidence, step 1
model.text: Every event SBD-DC01 forwards to the collector carries a timestamp from the clock you verified here; course 1.10 builds this path.

lessons.title: Find the time fault and record the fix
lessons.summary: Time faults rarely look like time: a refused sign-in, a replication error, a certificate that is suddenly not yet valid. Measure the offset first, find where the hierarchy broke — a member off its source, a moved PDC emulator role, a restored or reverted VM — then fix the cause, resync safely and record what happened.
steps: Recognize skew by its symptoms. Kerberos errors that name time — KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW, or 'There is a time and/or date difference between the client and server' at sign-in — access-denied errors in replication between the controllers, and certificates reported as not yet valid all point at a clock; if the controllers audit Kerberos failures, Security event 4771 with failure code 0x25 names the client. Measure before you change anything: w32tm /stripchart from the failing system to SBD-DC01 shows the offset.

Find out why a member left its source. Local CMOS Clock or Free-running System Clock means no usable source, a hypervisor provider means its host's time sync is on, and a peer name means someone set it by hand; a (Policy) value in w32tm /query /configuration points at a GPO, and events 129 and 36 show how long it has been adrift. Practice on the test client or SBD-DC02: set a manual peer with w32tm /config /manualpeerlist:SBD-DC01.sbd.test,0x8 /syncfromflags:manual /update, note that its time is still right but unauthenticated and off the hierarchy, then put it back with /syncfromflags:domhier.

Move the source with the PDC emulator role. When the role moves — a planned transfer, or a seizure after SBD-DC01 is lost — run w32tm /config /reliable:yes /update on the new holder and w32tm /config /syncfromflags:domhier /reliable:no /update on the old one, restart Windows Time on both, move the reference check to the new holder, and confirm that nltest /gtimeserv names it. Otherwise the old holder still advertises itself as the reliable source and the domain's time can keep flowing from a controller that is no longer the PDC emulator; practice only if you can move the role back the same day, because later courses expect SBD-DC01 to hold it.

Treat a restored or reverted VM as a clock problem as well as a directory one. It can come back with the clock it had when it was saved: members correct themselves, a domain controller corrects at most 48 hours each way (MaxPosPhaseCorrection and MaxNegPhaseCorrection) and logs an event instead, and SBD-DC01 has nothing to correct it at all, so every member follows its old time. After any restore or revert of SBD-DC01, compare it with the reference before you trust it.

Resync safely. On Windows, w32tm /resync /rediscover finds the source again and resynchronizes; on Linux, sudo chronyc makestep steps the clock once a controller is selectable. When an offset is beyond what the service will correct, set the clock close by hand first, correct SBD-DC01 only by the measured difference, and never point a system at an outside or manual source to make an error go away.

Record the fix like any other change: the symptom and when it started, the first offset measured, the cause, what you changed, the evidence that the chain is whole again — source, offset and events — and the rollback. A moved role also updates the time plan: who now runs the reference check, and the reverse procedure for when the role returns.
lessons.command:
# Measure before changing anything (on the failing system)
w32tm /stripchart /computer:SBD-DC01.sbd.test /samples:3 /dataonly
w32tm /query /source
w32tm /query /configuration | Select-String 'Type:|NtpServer:|\(Policy\)'
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; ProviderName='Microsoft-Windows-Time-Service'; Id=36,129} -MaxEvents 10 |
  Format-Table TimeCreated, Id -AutoSize
# Practice fault, then the fix (test client or SBD-DC02)
w32tm /config /manualpeerlist:SBD-DC01.sbd.test,0x8 /syncfromflags:manual /update
w32tm /query /source            # SBD-DC01.sbd.test,0x8: a manual peer, off the hierarchy
w32tm /config /syncfromflags:domhier /update
Restart-Service w32time
w32tm /resync /rediscover
w32tm /query /source            # a controller again
# If the PDC emulator role moves to SBD-DC02:
#   SBD-DC02: w32tm /config /reliable:yes /update; Restart-Service w32time
#   SBD-DC01: w32tm /config /syncfromflags:domhier /reliable:no /update; Restart-Service w32time
nltest /dsgetdc:sbd.test /gtimeserv   # must name the current PDC emulator
# Linux: sudo chronyc makestep, then chronyc tracking
lessons.check: The practice fault was found from the system's configuration before anything changed, the system names a controller again with Type NT5DS and an offset inside one second, nltest names the PDC emulator as the reliable source, and the record explains the cause rather than only showing a passing result.
lessons.evidence: Keep the fault record: the symptom and start time, the first offset, the source and configuration output before and after, the events, the change and its rollback, and the final offsets; after a role move, the updated time plan.
objectives: Recognize clock skew behind Kerberos, replication and certificate errors, and measure it before changing anything.
Return a member to the hierarchy, and move the time source with the PDC emulator role.
Resync safely after a restore or revert, and record the fix with its rollback.

quizzes.question: A member's source reads VM IC Time Synchronization Provider. What is wrong?
answers: Nothing: that is the domain hierarchy
SBD-DC01 has failed
The member takes its time from its hypervisor host instead of the domain; turn off that VM's host time sync
quizzes.explanation: A hypervisor provider means the host's clock, which the domain doesn't control, is setting the member's. Turn off the VM's host time sync and resync from the hierarchy.

quizzes.question: The PDC emulator role moved to SBD-DC02. What else must change?
answers: SBD-DC02 becomes the reliable source, SBD-DC01 returns to the domain hierarchy, and the reference check moves to SBD-DC02
Nothing: Windows Time follows the role on its own
Every member gets SBD-DC02 as a manual peer
quizzes.explanation: SBD-DC01 still carries AnnounceFlags 5 until you change it, so it would go on advertising itself as the reliable source. The configuration and the reference check must follow the role.

quizzes.question: SBD-DC01 was reverted to last week's checkpoint. Why compare it with the reference before anything else?
answers: Reverting removes its PDC emulator role
Nothing corrects the source itself: it serves whatever its clock says, and every member follows it
Kerberos tickets are stored in the checkpoint
quizzes.explanation: Members and SBD-DC02 correct toward SBD-DC01, so its error becomes everyone's. Only the reference check can catch it.

recap: Measure the offset first; a symptom only tells you which clock to look at.
A member off its source, a moved role and a restored VM each have their own fix.
Every fix is recorded with cause, evidence and rollback, and the time plan follows the role.
lessons.next: That completes Configure domain time. Course 1.4, Measure against the STIG, scans both controllers — and meets the one rule this design answers with a declared, checked clock.

model.label: Use a web app, step 2
model.text: The browser checks the certificate's validity dates against its own clock, so a client with the wrong time can refuse a certificate that is perfectly valid.
